trivia_fact: Netflix created Chaos Monkey in 2011 to randomly terminate virtual machine instances in production. The motivation was Netflix's migration to AWS — they needed confidence that their systems could survive the inherent unreliability of cloud infrastructure. The tool was open-sourced in 2012.

Netflix built an entire "Simian Army" of chaos tools: Chaos Monkey (kills instances), Chaos Gorilla (takes out an availability zone), Chaos Kong (simulates region failure), Latency Monkey (injects delays), Conformity Monkey (finds non-conforming instances), and Janitor Monkey (cleans unused resources).

The Principles of Chaos Engineering (principlesofchaos.org) were written in 2014 by Netflix engineers including Casey Rosenthal and Nora Jones. The document formalized chaos engineering as a discipline: define steady state, hypothesize, introduce real-world events, and look for differences.

Game days — planned exercises to test system resilience — borrow their name from military war games and disaster preparedness drills. Amazon popularized game days internally after the 2004 holiday season outages. Jesse Robbins, Amazon's "Master of Disaster," championed the practice.

Major AWS outages (S3 in 2017, us-east-1 in 2017 and 2020) actually helped justify chaos engineering budgets. Engineering managers could point to real multi-hour outages affecting thousands of companies and argue that proactive failure testing was cheaper than reactive recovery.

Gremlin Inc., founded in 2016 by former Netflix and Amazon engineers, built a venture-backed business around controlled chaos injection. The company offers "Failure as a Service" — a commercial platform for safely running chaos experiments without building custom tooling.

The "steady state hypothesis" is chaos engineering's key scientific concept. Before injecting failure, you define measurable indicators of normal system behavior (throughput, error rate, latency). The experiment tests whether the steady state holds under turbulent conditions, not whether the system "works."

LitmusChaos, created by MayaData (now part of the CNCF landscape), brought chaos engineering natively to Kubernetes. It uses custom resources (ChaosExperiments, ChaosEngines) to define and run chaos experiments as Kubernetes-native objects, fitting naturally into GitOps workflows.

The term "blast radius" in chaos engineering comes from explosives engineering. A core principle is starting with the smallest possible blast radius — one instance, one user, one request — and gradually expanding. Netflix calls this "minimizing the blast radius while maximizing learning."

Chaos engineering draws from Nassim Taleb's concept of "antifragility" — systems that get stronger from stress, not just survive it. The goal is not merely resilience (surviving failure) but antifragility (improving because of failure). Each experiment that reveals a weakness makes the system stronger once fixed.
